h1: Learning the brewery business before you sign a lease
title: Learn the Business Before the Lease | Craft Beer School
desc: Before you sign a brewery lease: work a shift, brew on someone else's kit, test demand and build the numbers. A low-risk route to your first brewery.
teaser: A lease is the first big commitment. The cheapest insurance is to learn the business before you sign.
standfirst: Most brewery failures are business failures: cash, pricing, volume and people. You can learn most of that before you commit to a building.
sections:
Spend time in a working brewery or taproom. Clean tanks, lift sacks, pour pints, watch a delivery. You see quickly what the job feels like and what the numbers mean on the ground. Many breweries welcome volunteers or part-time staff. A few weeks teaches more than a year of reading.

If you cannot work in one, visit several and ask the owners what surprised them most.

Ask to see a full brew day and a cleaning day. Ask what the owners wish they had known. The questions that bring out honest answers are about money and time: how long before the first profit, what the biggest unexpected cost was and what they would do differently with the lease.

You also learn whether you like the work. Brewing is physical, cold in the cellar, hot at the kettle and repetitive. Some people love it and some do not.

Contract or gypsy brewing lets you make beer on an existing brewhouse without owning one. You learn recipe scaling, scheduling, packaging and selling with a smaller risk. See starting a beer brand with contract brewing.

Treat it as a pilot with clear targets: how many litres, to whom, at what price and with what margin.

Keep records from the first brew: ingredients, volumes, losses, packaging, time, price and what sold. These records become the evidence in your business plan. A founder who can say what a litre cost on the last three batches is far more convincing than one who estimates.

Sell the beer at markets, to a few bars or through pre-orders. Note who buys it, how often and what they say. If you cannot sell a hundred litres, you will not sell ten thousand. Collect the facts that investors and landlords will ask for.

Test price as well as volume. Sell the same beer at two prices at different events and see what happens. Ask buyers why they chose it and whether they would buy it again next week. Repeat purchase matters more than a first sale.

Make a costing sheet for start-up costs, a monthly budget and a cash flow. Include rent, wages, duty, energy, packaging and the months before the first sale. Compare brewpub and production models with brewpub or production brewery and use start-up costs founders forget as a checklist.

If the sheet only works on perfect assumptions, change the plan.

Ask someone outside the business to check the sheet. An accountant, a lender or an experienced brewer will find what is missing. Do this before the lease, not after.

Add a worst-case column: sales at two thirds of plan, costs a tenth higher and the licence three months late. Check how long your cash lasts. If the answer is a few weeks, you need either more money or a smaller plan.

Share the sheet with someone who will challenge it. Friendly agreement teaches you nothing.

Understand the licensing chain for your country and how long it takes. See brewery licensing: the steps most countries share. Ask the regulator or a licensing adviser. Never sign a lease before you know the site can be licensed, or that you can leave if it cannot.

Talk to a licensing adviser early. Even a short conversation on the sequence, the timing and the conditions in your area can change your plan. It costs little compared with a lease on the wrong site.
Check the site and the lease

Walk the building with the checklist in choosing a brewery site. Ask a lawyer to read the lease. Ask for a break clause tied to licence approval. Negotiate rent-free months for fit-out where you can.

Then decide. Many people discover in this stage that they should start smaller, or not at all. That is a good result. It is far cheaper than finding out after the lease.

Keep your options open. A short lease, a shared brewery or a contract arrangement can bridge the gap while you prove demand. See what investors ask a brewery founder for what funders will want to see.
faqs: How long should I learn before I sign a lease?
There is no fixed time. Aim for enough experience to run the plant, a tested product and a costed plan. Many founders spend months to a year on it.
Can I learn without working in a brewery?
Yes, through courses, homebrewing, visits and contract brewing, but time in a working brewery is hard to replace.
What if I find out the model does not work?
That is a good outcome at this stage. Adjust the plan, start smaller or stop before you carry a lease.
